```{r}
#| label: knitr-opts

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(simevent)
library(survival)
```

simevent simulates event histories from a model of covariates, event processes
and the effects between them. As a running example, we simulate patients who may
relapse and die, and then use the model to evaluate a new drug.

# Starting Simple: Survival

Suppose we want to simulate how long patients survive, and that older patients
die sooner. `sim_model()` describes this with an age covariate, two processes,
and an effect of age on the death hazard. `sim_events()` then simulates patients
from the model:

```{r}
#| label: survival-model

survival_model <- sim_model(
  age = sim_covariate(function(N) rnorm(N, mean = 60, sd = 10)),
  censoring = sim_process("censoring", eta = 0.05, nu = 1),
  death = sim_process("terminal", eta = 0.05, nu = 1.2),
  effects = list(sim_effect(death ~ age - 60, coef = 0.04))
)
survival_model

survival_data <- sim_events(survival_model, n = 2000, seed = 1)
head(survival_data)
```

Each patient is followed until death or censoring. The death hazard is

$$
  \lambda_{\text{death}}(t)
  = \lambda_0(t) \exp\left( 0.04 (\text{age} - 60) \right),
$$

where $\lambda_0(t)$ is the baseline hazard given by `eta` and `nu`, so each
year above 60 raises the hazard by about 4%.

::: {.callout-note title="Baseline hazards"}
`eta` and `nu` are the Weibull scale and shape. To use a given curve instead,
pass a cumulative baseline hazard as `cumhaz`.
:::

# Adding Treatment

Now suppose older patients are more likely to be treated, and treatment lowers
the death hazard. Treatment is another covariate, one that depends on age, and
`update()` adds it to the existing model:

```{r}
#| label: treatment-model

treatment_model <- update(
  survival_model,
  treatment = sim_covariate(function(N, age) {
    rbinom(N, 1, plogis((age - 60) / 10))
  }),
  effects = list(sim_effect(death ~ treatment, coef = -0.5))
)
treatment_model
```

::: {.callout-note title="Covariates and terms"}
A covariate's function takes `N` and any covariates defined earlier, matched by
argument name. `+` separates the terms of an effect, each with its own `coef`,
as in `sim_effect(death ~ age + treatment, coef = c(0.04, -0.5))`. To give a sum
one `coef`, wrap it in parentheses.
:::

# Adding Relapse

Patients can also relapse, possibly several times, and each relapse raises the
death hazard. Treatment makes relapse less likely. A relapse doesn't end
follow-up, so it's a `"transient"` process, and using its name in an effect
gives the patient's number of relapses so far:

```{r}
#| label: relapse-model

relapse_model <- update(
  treatment_model,
  relapse = sim_process("transient", eta = 0.3, nu = 1),
  effects = list(
    sim_effect(relapse ~ treatment, coef = -0.7),
    sim_effect(death ~ relapse, coef = 0.5)
  )
)

relapse_data <- sim_events(relapse_model, n = 2000, seed = 1)
head(relapse_data)
```

Each row is now an event, and `plot_event_data()` shows the histories:

```{r}
#| label: relapse-plot

plot_event_data(relapse_data[relapse_data$id <= 100, ], title = "Relapse Data")
```

::: {.callout-note title="Reading the data"}
The `relapse` column is the count *after* each row's event. For the values
during each interval, as needed for a Cox model, use `interval_format_data()`.
To cap the number of relapses, use `sim_process()`'s `limit`.
:::

# Effects of Event History

So far every relapse adds the same amount to the log-hazard, forever. Suppose
instead that a third relapse is especially serious, and that the risk is highest
right after a relapse and then fades. Both can be written directly in the
formula, using the current time `t` and `event_time()`:

```{r}
#| label: history-model

history_model <- update(
  relapse_model,
  effects = list(
    sim_effect(death ~ relapse >= 3, coef = 1),
    sim_effect(
      death ~ (relapse > 0) * exp(-(t - event_time(relapse, -1))),
      coef = 1.5
    )
  )
)
```

::: {.callout-note title="`event_time()` before the event"}
`event_time(proc, k)` is the time of `proc`'s `k`-th event, or `k`-th latest if
`k` is negative, and `0` if it hasn't happened yet. Without `(relapse > 0) *`,
patients who haven't relapsed would have `exp(-t)`, as if they had relapsed at
time 0.
:::

With all effects so far, the death hazard is

$$
  \begin{aligned}
    \lambda_{\text{death}}(t) = \lambda_0(t) \exp\Big(
     & 0.04 (\text{age} - 60) - 0.5 \, \text{treatment} + 0.5 R(t) \\
     & + \mathbf{1}\{R(t) \ge 3\}
    + 1.5 \cdot \mathbf{1}\{R(t) > 0\} \cdot e^{-(t-T_{\text{last}}(t))} \Big),
  \end{aligned}
$$

where $R(t)$ is the number of relapses so far and $T_{\text{last}}(t)$ the time
of the latest one, `event_time(relapse, -1)`. For an untreated 60-year-old who
relapses at times 2, 4 and 7, this gives:

```{r}
#| label: history-hazard
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Line chart of the death hazard relative to baseline over time, on a log
#|   scale. It is flat at 1 until the first relapse, jumps at each relapse and
#|   then fades towards a higher level, with the largest rise at the third.

relapse_times <- c(2, 4, 7)
time <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.01)
relapses_so_far <- findInterval(time, relapse_times)
latest_relapse <- c(0, relapse_times)[relapses_so_far + 1]

relative_hazard <- exp(
  0.5 * relapses_so_far +
    (relapses_so_far >= 3) +
    1.5 * (relapses_so_far > 0) * exp(-(time - latest_relapse))
)

plot(
  time,
  relative_hazard,
  type = "l",
  log = "y",
  lwd = 2,
  las = 1,
  bty = "l",
  xlab = "Time",
  ylab = "Death hazard relative to baseline"
)
abline(v = relapse_times, lty = 2, col = "grey60")
```

Each relapse (dashed lines) raises the hazard sharply, and it then fades towards
a level higher than before.

See `vignette("event-times-and-markers")` for more effect shapes, and for
covariates that are re-measured over time.

# Estimating Intervention Effects

Suppose a new drug halves the relapse hazard. What would that do to mortality?
`sim_events()`'s `intervene` argument multiplies a process's hazard, so simulate
with and without the drug, with censoring off (`cens = 0`), and compare the runs
with `event_risk()`:

```{r}
#| label: drug-risk

natural <- sim_events(history_model, n = 2000, cens = 0, seed = 1)
drug <- sim_events(
  history_model,
  n = 2000,
  cens = 0,
  intervene = list(relapse = 0.5),
  seed = 1
)

outcomes <- c("relapse", "death")
data.frame(
  process = outcomes,
  natural = event_risk(natural, history_model, outcomes, tau = 5)$risk,
  drug = event_risk(drug, history_model, outcomes, tau = 5)$risk
)
```

The drug lowers the 5-year risk of a first relapse and, since relapses raise the
death hazard, the risk of death too. `type = "time_lost"` gives the expected
years lost before `tau` instead:

```{r}
#| label: drug-time-lost

event_risk(drug, history_model, "death", tau = 5, type = "time_lost")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Intervening on a covariate"}
`intervene` can also fix covariates. Suppose we want the effect of treatment on
death. Comparing treated and untreated patients is confounded by age, because
older patients are more often treated. Instead, we can simulate the same
population with no one treated, and with everyone treated:

```{r}
#| label: treatment-contrast

treat_none <- sim_events(
  history_model,
  n = 2000,
  cens = 0,
  intervene = list(treatment = 0),
  seed = 1
)
treat_all <- sim_events(
  history_model,
  n = 2000,
  cens = 0,
  intervene = list(treatment = 1),
  seed = 1
)

by_group <- event_risk(
  natural,
  history_model,
  "death",
  tau = 5,
  by = "treatment"
)
data.frame(
  treatment = by_group$treatment,
  compared = by_group$risk,
  intervened = c(
    event_risk(treat_none, history_model, "death", tau = 5)$risk,
    event_risk(treat_all, history_model, "death", tau = 5)$risk
  )
)
```

The direct comparison (`compared`) understates the benefit of treatment, because
the treated patients are older and so at higher risk to begin with.

`by` only takes baseline columns. For a `sim_mark()`, group by its baseline
value `<mark>_0`.
:::

## Calibrating a Coefficient

So far we've chosen the effect of relapse on death ourselves. Suppose instead
that we want the effect needed for the drug to prevent 5 percentage points of
deaths within 5 years. To find it, we write the drug's effect as a function of
the coefficient, using `update()` to replace the `death ~ relapse` effect in
`relapse_model`:

```{r}
#| label: calibration-objective

drug_effect <- function(coef, n = 3000, tau = 5, seed = 1) {
  model <- update(
    relapse_model,
    effects = list(sim_effect(death ~ relapse, coef = coef))
  )

  natural <- sim_events(model, n = n, cens = 0, seed = seed)
  drug <- sim_events(
    model,
    n = n,
    cens = 0,
    intervene = list(relapse = 0.5),
    seed = seed
  )

  event_risk(natural, model, "death", tau = tau)$risk -
    event_risk(drug, model, "death", tau = tau)$risk
}
```

Any (black-box) optimization method can then be used, below we use `uniroot()`:

```{r}
#| label: calibration-uniroot

sapply(c(0, 0.5, 1, 2), drug_effect)

calibrated <- uniroot(
  function(coef) drug_effect(coef) - 0.05,
  interval = c(0, 2),
  tol = 0.01
)
```

So the drug prevents 5 percentage points of deaths if each relapse multiplies
the death hazard by about `{r} round(exp(calibrated$root), 1)`.

# Building a `sim_model()` from Fitted Cox Models

So far we've chosen every effect ourselves. If you have observed data, you can
instead fit a `coxph()` model for each process, and `sim_model_from_fits()` then
builds a `sim_model()` from the fits. Here we use `relapse_data` as the observed
data:

```{r}
#| label: fits-model

observed <- interval_format_data(relapse_data, proc_cols = "relapse")

fits <- list(
  censoring = coxph(
    Surv(tstart, tstop, event == "censoring") ~ age,
    data = observed
  ),
  relapse = coxph(
    Surv(tstart, tstop, event == "relapse") ~ treatment,
    data = observed
  ),
  death = coxph(
    Surv(tstart, tstop, event == "death") ~ age + treatment + relapse,
    data = observed
  )
)
types <- c(censoring = "censoring", relapse = "transient", death = "terminal")

fitted_model <- sim_model_from_fits(fits, observed, types)
fitted_model
```

The coefficients are close to those of `relapse_model`. Simulating from the
fitted model gives a similar mix of events:

```{r}
#| label: fits-simulate

new_data <- sim_events(fitted_model, n = 2000, seed = 2)

event_levels <- levels(new_data$event)
rbind(
  observed = prop.table(table(factor(relapse_data$event, event_levels))),
  simulated = prop.table(table(new_data$event))
)
```

The fitted model can then be used for everything above, such as evaluating the
drug.

::: {.callout-note title="What `sim_model_from_fits()` assumes"}
- Baseline covariates are resampled as whole rows of `data`, which keeps the
  relationships between them.
- Each process uses its fit's cumulative baseline hazard. It's unknown after the
  last observed time, so follow-up ends there, with `event = "max_cens"`.
- A variable named after a process, like `relapse` here, is that process's event
  count.
- A categorical covariate must be a factor column in `data`, used directly in
  the formula, not wrapped in `factor()`.
:::
